extracted.intended_audience: general readers/colonists sympathetic to or undecided about American independence
extracted.subtask_description: A persuasive 18th-century pamphlet (Thomas Paine's Common Sense) arguing for separation from Great Britain and critiquing monarchy and hereditary succession. It aims to convince ordinary colonists by plain argument, scripture, history, and appeals to self-interest and posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy is a harmful and unnecessary form of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Government by kings was first introduced by the Heathens and is described as 'the most prosperous invention the Devil ever set on foot for the promotion of idolatry.' The pamphlet argues monarchy degrades mankind, promotes idolatrous homage, and cannot be justified by nature or scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and rhetoric: 'How impious is the title of sacred Majesty applied to a worm,' and the claim that monarchy is 'the popery of government.' The text contrasts peaceful republican/tribal early societies (e.g., early Patriarchs, Holland) with monarchies, asserting kings throw mankind into confusion and produce war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession is unjust and an imposition on posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because all men are originally equal, no one can claim by birth a perpetual right for his descendants to rule; hereditary right is an insult and imposition on future generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: 'no one by birth could have a right to set up his own family in perpetual preference to all others' and the natural proof of folly that 'nature disapproves it... by giving mankind an Ass for a Lion.' Also notes that what began as convenience became claimed as right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy produces war, oppression, and social disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: The pride and prerogatives of kings are said to throw mankind into confusion and lead to wars; absence of kings correlates with greater peace (example: Holland). Monarchy and hereditary succession have 'laid the world in blood and ashes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evidence cited: English history with many civil wars and rebellions since the conquest; the Wars of the Roses (York vs Lancaster) as illustration of hereditary contest leading to bloodshed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy promotes idolatry and impious public homage
rubrics_metrics.description: Heathens paid divine honours to deceased kings and monarchies continued/improved this worship of living rulers, which the pamphlet treats as impious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetoric: the application of titles like 'sacred Majesty' to mortal men is condemned; scripture and religious objections are used to denounce royal exaltation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture and religious history disapprove of government by kings
rubrics_metrics.description: Biblical episodes (Gideon, Samuel and the Israelites) are invoked to show that the will of the Almighty disapproves monarchy; monarchy is ranked among the sins of the Jews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual citations and narrative: Samuel's warning about the manner of kings (taking sons, daughters, fields, tithes) is used as explicit scriptural evidence against monarchy: 'AND THE LORD WILL NOT HEAR YOU IN THAT DAY.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy breeds bribery, corruption, favoritism, and economic exaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of kings is described as taking sons for chariots, daughters for cooks, fields and vineyards for servants, and taking tithes — portraying bribery, corruption, favouritism and economic burden as standing vices of kings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct quotation/paraphrase of Samuel's prophecy about kings: 'He will take your sons...appoint them for his chariots...he will take the tenth of your seed...and ye shall be his servants.' Used as a catalogue of monarchic abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession does not ensure wise rulers and cultivates arrogance
rubrics_metrics.description: Those raised to rule from birth tend to grow insolent and ignorant of the interests of the general population; selection by birth often produces rulers 'the most ignorant and unfit of any throughout the dominions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological/social claim: being 'selected from the rest of mankind' poisons minds by importance and reduces exposure to common life, producing unfit governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession heightens risks from minorities and regencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The throne may fall to a minor, producing regencies that betray trust, and aged or infirm monarchs can render the public prey to miscreants who manipulate weakness or infancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific harms noted: opportunities for betrayal under regency and national misfortune when a king is too old or too young to rule effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession does not prevent civil wars; it fosters them
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to the plea that hereditary succession preserves peace, English history shows numerous civil wars and rebellions under hereditary monarchy; succession contests provoke prolonged bloodshed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited: 'Thirty kings and two minors...eight civil wars and nineteen Rebellions' since the conquest; the Wars of the Roses as an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: In many monarchies, the king's actual business is limited and often harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: In England, a king largely 'maketh war and giveth away places' — roles which impoverish the nation and promote faction rather than public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: in absolute monarchies the king may bear all civil and military business, but in England his practical role is narrow and damaging; rhetorical condemnation of lavish royal expense and worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: The republican element (Commons) embodies true English liberty but is corrupted by the Crown
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons represents the republican part of the constitution and the liberty people boast of, but the corrupt influence of the Crown (control of places) has swallowed up its power and 'eaten out the virtue' of the Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim that England's constitution is 'sickly' because monarchy has 'poisoned the Republic' and 'engrossed the Commons,' implying that defense of liberty requires restoring republican virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: America's welfare requires separation from Great Britain; dependence brings many injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Connection and dependence on Britain involve the colonies in European wars, ruin trade during conflict, and benefit Britain more than America; thus separation better secures America's commerce, peace, and future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: Britain protected America from self-interest; separation would allow neutral commerce with Europe; 'any submission...tends directly to involve this Continent in European wars' and 'not a single advantage is derived' from the connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Britain's protection was motivated by interest not attachment; alliances are risky
rubrics_metrics.description: Britain defended the colonies out of interest (trade/domination), not out of regard for Americans; similar motives would apply in other theatres, so relying on British 'protection' is fallacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: Britain would defend Turkey for trade; colonial dependence may drag America into distant conflicts and is not a trustworthy foundation for security.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'parent country' metaphor is manipulative and misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling Britain the 'parent' or 'mother country' is a rhetorical trick to bias colonists; in truth America was peopled by refugees from all Europe and 'Europe, and not England, is the parent country of America.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polemic: the phrase is 'jesuitically adopted' to gain bias; the pamphlet urges readers to reject the narrow sentimental appeal and see broader continental ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: The shift to armed conflict makes prior reconciliation plans obsolete
rubrics_metrics.description: Once hostilities began (after April 19), all plans and proposals that aimed at union or reconciliation before that date are 'like the almanacks of the last year' — proper then but now superseded and useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for political strategy: the appeal to arms changes the political landscape and demands new thinking; previous advocates' proposals should be reconsidered in light of the new era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincing argumentation requires divesting prejudice and using plain reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The author requests that readers 'divest himself of prejudice and prepossession, and suffer his reason and his feelings to determine for themselves' — advocating simple facts, plain arguments, and common sense as the mode of persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style and rhetorical guidance: appeal to common-sense, remove bias, and consider posterity; the pamphlet models a plain, accessible argumentative style aimed at ordinary readers.
